paras: Every year, Dr. Laura Mendes interviews about two hundred students who want to study medicine, and she asks almost all of them the same question: should a doctor ever tell a patient, “I am not sure”? She says the answers tell her more than any grade. Three candidates from last year show why.

The first candidate answered in under ten seconds. “Absolutely not. A doctor must clearly know the answer. There is no question that patients want certainty.” As far as Dr. Mendes could tell, he was not lying. He simply overstated everything. By the end of the interview, every claim sounded the same size, so none of them carried any weight. “When everything is obvious,” she says, “nothing is.”

The second candidate went the other way. “I suppose it might perhaps depend, possibly, on the situation.” Her answers were so tentative that the panel could not infer what she actually believed. She never said anything false, but she never really said anything at all, and that, too, cost her credibility.

The third candidate did something different. “I am convinced that patients deserve the truth,” he said. “Whether a doctor should say ‘I am not sure’ is harder. The evidence seems to suggest that patients trust doctors more when they admit uncertainty, though I may be wrong about how that works in Brazil.” He was firm about his values, which are subjective, and careful about the facts, which should be objective. “He left room for doubt exactly where doubt belonged,” Dr. Mendes says. “If anything, the hedge made him sound more sure of himself, not less.” He never implied that he knew everything, and that is why she believed the rest.
reading.source: A composite account of medical school admissions interviews, written for this lesson.

items.situation: Give your opinion about the vestibular, starting with: I am convinced that...
tips: I am convinced that the vestibular rewards discipline more than talent.
A booster is for what you really believe, not for facts you cannot prove.

items.situation: Make this softer, with one hedge: Sport makes students better at studying.
tips: Sport arguably makes students better at studying.
One hedge is enough. Two start to sound lost.

items.situation: Make this stronger. It is about your own goal: It might be possible that I want to be a surgeon.
tips: I definitely want to be a surgeon.
Your own goals deserve a booster. A hedge makes them sound borrowed.

items.situation: Open a sentence about your cursinho year with a stance adverb.
tips: Surprisingly, the hardest part of the year has not been the content.
The adverb shows your attitude before the content arrives.

items.situation: Say something about Brazilian hospitals that you are not completely sure about.
tips: As far as I can tell, the biggest problem is the waiting time, but I may be wrong.
A fact you cannot prove gets a hedge, not a booster.

items.situation: Correct this out loud: Obviously, I think that maybe this is clearly true.
tips: I think this is probably true.
Never put a hedge and a booster on the same claim.

listenings.text: When I started working as a doctor, I thought patients wanted certainty, so I spoke as if I had it. Clearly, this is a virus. There is no question it will pass. Then one of those viruses turned out to be something else, and I learned what overstating costs. The patient did not stop trusting that diagnosis. She stopped trusting me. Today I talk differently. I say, this is most likely a virus, and if you are not better in three days, I want to see you again. Interestingly, patients do not hear that as weakness. As far as I can tell, they hear it as honesty. The hedge tells them exactly how sure I am, and that is the one thing they really need to know.

Students preparing for the TOEFL usually make one of two mistakes in the opinion tasks. The first group hedges everything, because they think it sounds academic. Their answers are full of might, perhaps and it could be argued, and by the end the examiner has no idea what they actually think. The second group boosts everything. Obviously this, undoubtedly that, and after a while nothing sounds important. My advice is simple. Take a clear position in your first sentence, and boost it. I firmly believe that. Then hedge your evidence, because evidence is rarely perfect. Research suggests. It seems that. Your opinion should sound certain, and your facts should sound careful. Students who do this usually gain points without learning a single new word.
